opus-5.5.text:
It's been a really interesting thing to watch, because for a long time it felt like we were making a somewhat contrarian bet. When Cohere started, the conviction was that language was going to be the interface, that the way people interact with technology, and the way businesses get value out of all the unstructured text they're sitting on, would fundamentally run through models that understand and generate language. At the time, a lot of people saw that as a fairly niche research direction, or something that was still years away from being practically useful.

So in some ways the sudden wave of public interest feels less like a surprise and more like the rest of the world catching up to something that people inside the field had been seeing build for a while. The capabilities didn't appear overnight. There were years of steady progress in scaling, in training techniques, in alignment and instruction tuning. What changed was really the interface. Once people could just talk to a model directly, the progress became tangible to everyone, not just researchers reading papers.

For me, coming from the research side, what's exciting is that the attention brings a lot of new questions to the forefront. When it's a research curiosity, you can afford to focus mostly on benchmark performance. Once these models are in front of millions of people, you have to care much more about things like efficiency, reliability, how models behave across different languages and cultures, and who actually gets served well by these systems. A lot of my own interest has been in those questions, like what happens in the long tail, which languages get left behind, and how you make these models work under real-world constraints.

So I see the relationship as validation of the original focus, but also as a responsibility. The interest is enormous right now, and the challenge is making sure the technology actually lives up to it in a way that's useful and broadly accessible, rather than just impressive in a demo.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Cohere’s language focus began as a contrarian bet and describes the surge in public interest as the rest of the world catching up, indicating the original focus predated and was not a response to that surge.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually been fascinating to watch, because Cohere was founded on the premise that large language models were going to matter, and that was before it was obvious to most people. Aidan was one of the authors on the original transformer paper, and the bet from the beginning was that this architecture, scaled up and trained on huge amounts of text, was going to unlock something fundamentally different in how people interact with computers. So in some ways the sudden wave of interest feels like validation of a thesis the company has had from day one.

But I'd also say the attention has changed what the work looks like. When I joined and we started Cohere For AI, the research community was already quite convinced of the importance of these models, but the public conversation was much narrower. Now you have people who have never thought about machine learning asking questions about hallucination, about where the training data comes from, about what languages these models actually serve. And I think that's healthy. It brings a lot more scrutiny, and it forces us to be honest about what we know and what we don't.

For me personally, the part I find most interesting is that the hype tends to concentrate around a very small slice of what language models could be. It's mostly English, it's mostly chat interfaces, it's mostly a handful of benchmarks. And a lot of our research effort is really about the gaps in that picture: how these models behave across languages, how robust they are, how we evaluate them in ways that actually reflect how people use them. So I view the public interest as a huge opportunity, but also a responsibility to widen the conversation beyond the narrow set of things that happen to be getting attention right now.

r001.rationale: The response says Cohere was founded on the premise that large language models would matter before that was obvious to most people, framing later public interest as validation of its original thesis.

astra-6.text:
I think the public interest caught up with something that had been motivating the work for a long time. Language is such a natural way for us to communicate, so it’s also a very powerful way to make technology accessible. Cohere’s focus on language preceded this wave of attention; it wasn’t a response to it.

What changed was that people could interact with these models directly and get an intuitive sense of what they could do. That’s a very different experience from hearing about a research result. But there’s still a gap between that first moment of excitement and making these systems useful and reliable in practice. For me, that’s where a lot of the interesting work is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Cohere’s focus on language preceded the wave of attention and “wasn’t a response to it.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think, in some ways, the public interest caught up with something Cohere had been focused on for a long time. Language was central from the beginning. It’s how we communicate, but it’s also how so much of the information within an organization is represented, so making that information useful is a very powerful opportunity.

What changed with this wave of interest is that people could interact with these models directly and immediately get a sense of what they could do. You didn’t need to be a machine learning researcher to see the potential. But there’s still a lot of work between that initial excitement and making these systems useful and reliable in practice. So I see it less as a change in direction and more as a much broader recognition of why that original focus matters.

r001.rationale: The response says Cohere had been focused on language for a long time and that public interest caught up with that original focus, indicating it did not arise in response to the later surge.
